title: Ibero-American countries back human oversight for AI decisions that affect people
excerpt: Ministers meeting in Madrid on 3 November 2026 agreed that people must supervise AI used for significant decisions, and set up a voluntary regional AI alliance.

body_html:
Governments from across Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula have agreed a shared set of principles for artificial intelligence, including a commitment that people supervise AI when it is used for decisions with significant effects on someone's life.

The principles are set out in a declaration adopted on 3 November 2026 in Madrid by ministers responsible for digital transformation and AI from the Ibero-American community. That community is a group of 22 Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries in the Americas and Europe that meets at regular summits. The ministers' meeting prepared the 30th Ibero-American Summit of heads of state and government, also held in Madrid on 4 and 5 November.

What the declaration says

The declaration, published by Spain's Ministry for Digital Transformation, commits the signing governments to:

  • Human supervision of AI used in decisions with significant effects on people, in line with each country's laws.
  • Clear responsibility: transparency, proportionate traceability, and responsibilities that can be clearly identified.
  • Cybersecurity as part of developing AI safely, and action against fraud, impersonation and other deceptive uses of AI.
  • Children and teenagers: digital spaces suited to each age group, with privacy and security built in by design.
  • Fair treatment: environments free of bias, and non-discrimination in access to and use of technology.
  • Personal data protection and privacy by design.

It also states a principle familiar from human rights law: "Rights and freedoms recognised in the analogue world must also be respected in digital environments" (Humasure's translation from the Spanish).

Ministers adopted two regional reference standards, one on data protection and one on digital identity and interoperability in government services. Both are explicitly non-binding.

A voluntary AI alliance

The ministers also approved an Ibero-American Alliance for Artificial Intelligence and sent it to the summit for adoption. Spain's government listed the alliance among the new agreements of the summit's closing session on 5 November.

According to the declaration, the alliance has three parts: a shared data space in which each country keeps control of its own data; AI models that work well in Spanish, Portuguese and, over time, Indigenous and other official languages; and fairer access to high-performance computing for public-interest projects. Participation is voluntary, and the declaration describes the cooperation as gradual and flexible.

What is not yet known

  • Which countries will join. The declaration invites countries to join after the summit. Reports differ on how many took part: one report counts 20 nations, another 22 member states.
  • Funding. One analysis of the summit notes that no binding funding commitments were reported.
  • How oversight will be applied. The declaration sets principles, not rules. Human supervision is to follow each country's own legal framework, so what it means in practice will vary.

Argentina and Paraguay dissociated themselves from the ministerial declaration, according to the text.

Why it matters for people staying in charge

Several countries in the region are still debating AI laws: Brazil's AI bill has passed the Senate but not the Chamber of Deputies, and Chile's AI bill is still open to amendment. A shared statement that people must supervise AI in decisions that matter, and that someone must be clearly responsible, gives citizens, regulators and companies a common starting point across more than 20 countries.

These commitments line up with several of the 10 Humasure Directives: human supervision with D1 Always stoppable; clear responsibility with D9 Accountable; privacy by design with D5 Private by default; cybersecurity with D6 Secure and supported; and non-discrimination with D8 Fair treatment.

Principles are a first step. The test will be whether they become clear, checkable requirements, so that a person affected by an AI decision can find out who supervised it and how to challenge it.
